paragraphs.text: Here Jeremiah, in the name and place of all the Jewish people, setteth forth his sufferings very passionately and elegantly. Oυδεν γαρ του παθοντος ρητορικοτερον, saith Synesius; for nothing is more rhetorical than a man in misery. See on Lam 1:12.
paragraphs.anchor: I am the man.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Of God’s wrath, whom yet he nameth not prae magnitudine affectus, {a} but referreth to him all his sufferings; and he alludeth here, say some, to that rod. {Jer 1:11}
paragraphs.anchor: By the rod of his wrath

paragraphs.text: {a} Oecolamp.

Perstat semper in metaphora a pastoritia, say some, who by rod in the foregoing verse understand God’s shepherd’s wand, wherewith, when he is displeased, he driveth his unruly sheep into dark and dangerous places. {Psa 23:3-4 Mic 7:9}
paragraphs.anchor: He hath led me and brought me into darkness.

paragraphs.text: Metaphora a colaphizantibus. A metaphor from buffeters, who double their blows, beating their adversaries on both sides, as the smith doth his red hot iron upon the anvil till he hath shaped it. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: Surely against me is he turned.

paragraphs.text: {a} Hinc inde continenter verberat. - Jun.
Withered it and wanzed it, so that I am not like myself; facta videbor anus, as she said. See Psa 32:3.
paragraphs.anchor: My flesh and my skin hath he made old.

paragraphs.text: Decayed and impaired, and that with greatest torment, as befalleth when bones are broken.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath broken my bones.

paragraphs.text: Bulwarks and batteries.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath builded against me.

paragraphs.text: Or, With venom and vexation. See Jer 8:14. In these and the like hyperbolic expressions we must note that words are too weak to utter the greatness of the saints’ grief, when they lie under the sense of God’s wrath and heavy displeasure.
paragraphs.anchor: And compassed me with gall and travel.

paragraphs.text: Dungeons haply, which are a kind of graves, and where poor prisoners lie as forgotten. The Persians called their prisons ληθας, oblivions. And Ezekiel saith that Babylon was to the Jews as a grave, where they lay for dead till those dead bones lived again. {Eze 37:1-14}
paragraphs.anchor: He hath set me in dark places.

paragraphs.text: Free among the dead and forgotten. It may be said of a saint, in some cases, that
paragraphs.anchor: As they that be dead of old.

paragraphs.text: “ Vivit, et est vitae nescius ipse sum. ”
Sorrounded me with troubles, brought me into straits inextricable and importable.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath hedged me about.

paragraphs.text: As poor prisoners use to do for relief and release.
paragraphs.anchor: Also when I cry and shout.

paragraphs.text: Or, Shutteth his ear to my prayer. This was very grievous to any good heart; more than it could be to Cicero, a stranger to the true God, who yet bewaileth the matter to his brother in these words, I would pray to the gods for those things; but that, alas! they have given over to hear my prayers.
paragraphs.anchor: He shutteth out my prayer.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Most strongly and closely, so that none can come at me.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath enclosed my ways with hewn stone

paragraphs.text: So that all things go cross with me; and although they were never so well devised, yet still they sort out unto the worst.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath made all my paths crooked.

paragraphs.text: So that if I do but offer to stir, or seek to make escape, I am in danger to be devoured.
paragraphs.anchor: He was unto me as a bear lying in wait.

paragraphs.text: God hath many ways and means to bemeet with sinners. He can stop them in their course, as he did Balaam, Jonah, and others.
paragraphs.anchor: And as a lion in secret places.

paragraphs.text: As Lam 3:9.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath turned aside my ways.

paragraphs.text: As a bear or lion doth the silly sheep that falleth into their paws. Carnali quadam intemperie haec effusa sunt. The Vulgate hath it, Confregit me. He hath broken me in pieces; scil., Attempting to leap over his hedge; {Lam 3:7} his stone wall. {Lam 3:9} In the year 1590, Nicolas Frischlin, that famous poet, orator, and philosopher, attempting to escape out of prison, was so broken, a capite ad talos, a cute ad ossa. from the head to the heels, from the skin to the bones. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: And pulled me in pieces.

paragraphs.text: {a} Alsted., Chron., 480.
Lam 2:4.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath bent his bow.

paragraphs.text: Which he is sure to hit. The Benjamites, {Jdg 20:16} the Parthians, Alcon the Cretan, Domitian the Emperor, were excellent archers; but
paragraphs.anchor: And set me as a mark.

paragraphs.text: “ Non semper feriet quodcunque minabitur arcus; ”
God’s arrow never misseth the mark.
{a} Heb., The sons of his quiver, by a Hebraism. So Horace hath -
paragraphs.anchor: He hath caused the arrows of his quiver to enter into my reins.

paragraphs.text: “ Pharetram gravidam sagittis. ” - Lib, ii. od. 21.
“Full quiver of arrows.”
Job hath many like complaints. {Job 7:20; Job 8:4; Job 16:12-13}
{a} Renes sunt sedes libidinis.
Or, To all peoples. Our Saviour suffered all this and much more for us.
paragraphs.anchor: I was a derision, to all my people.

paragraphs.text: Or, Their lute, or kit, whom they played on at pleasure, and desired no better sport.
paragraphs.anchor: And their song all the day.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Bitternesses: {a} alluding, as some think, to that ius seu embamma in quo intingebant agnum Paschalem, sauce of bitter herbs wherewith they did eat the Passover - the juice of them expressed - to mind them of the bitter afflictions which they suffered in Egypt.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath filled me with bitterness.

paragraphs.text: Or, Hensbane, or wolfsbane rather, succo cicutae.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath made me drunk with wormwood.

paragraphs.text: {a} Exarescunt torrentes, metalla exhauriuntur, flumina deficiunt, prata item cum structibus, &c.
Comminuit scrupis dentes meos - i.e., With gritty bread. See Pro 20:17.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath also broken my teeth with gravel stones.

paragraphs.text: The Greek and Latin have it, He hath fed me with ashes, which was worse than that bread made most of sawdust, wherewith they fed the martyrs in the Marian times.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath covered me with ashes.

paragraphs.text: Prosperity and I are twain; we are utterly unacquainted.
paragraphs.anchor: And thou hast removed my soul far off from peace.

paragraphs.text: But not so wisely. I was even almost tumbling into the pit of desperation. I was straddling over it, as it were, but God preserved me.
paragraphs.anchor: And I said.

paragraphs.text: My strength to bear these miseries, and my hope to be ever freed of them.
paragraphs.anchor: My strength and my hope is perished.

paragraphs.text: i.e., The bitterness that was in it, but of mine own commingling. Impatiens quisque bis affligitur, Impatience redoubleth an affliction.
paragraphs.anchor: Remembering mine affliction and my misery, the wormwood and the gall

paragraphs.text: But it is not good to plod overly much in this case. Such bitter pills should be swallowed whole, and not chewed upon, unless it be for our further humiliation.
paragraphs.anchor: My soul hath them still in remembrance.

paragraphs.text: This? What? God’s infinite mercies, that cape of good hope; see Lam 3:22 Psa 119:56; "This I had" - that is, this comfort, or this ability to keep thy precepts.
paragraphs.anchor: This I recall to my mind.

paragraphs.text: It is of the Lord’s mercy that we are not consumed.] That we are yet on this side hell. This sentence was much in the mouth of that famous Maria Aegyptiaca, and should be in all our minds and mouths for a lenitive.

Because his compassions fail {a} not.] Or, Are not spent, wasted, but, as the oil in the cruse, as the spring ever runneth, the sun ever shineth, &c. This should ever shine in our hearts as the sun doth in the firmament.
{a} Exarescunt torrentes, metalla exhauriuntur, flumina deficiunt, prata item cum fructibus, &c.
Yea, every moment. We have continual experiments.
paragraphs.anchor: They are new every morning.

paragraphs.text: God’s mercy moved him to promise; his truth to perform. See 2Sa 7:18; 2Sa 7:21. {See Trapp on "2Sa 7:18"} {See Trapp on "2Sa 7:21"}
paragraphs.anchor: Great is thy faithfulness.

paragraphs.text: And that is enough for me, should I never have more. {See Trapp on "Psa 16:5"} That which giveth content in any portion is (1.) The favour and presence of God; (2.) That it is from the hand of a Father; (3.) That it comes to us in the covenant of grace; (4.) That it is the purchase of Christ’s blood; (5.) That it is an answer of prayers, and a blessing from above on honest endeavours, &c. Vide autem, pie Lector, saith an expositor: See here, good reader, how this prophetic lamentation beginneth to be a guide to godliness.
paragraphs.anchor: The Lord is my portion.

paragraphs.text: For it doth not, after the manner of silly women, throw out empty words without wisdom; but teacheth all along, either overtly or covertly, that all things here below, how highly soever esteemed, are vanity and soon lost; but the grace of God is solid and stable; {a} Christum tollere nemo potest. Christ is a portion unlosable, as one {b} once answered to those that asked him why he was still merry and cheerful.
{c} Not my mouth only; but I speak it from my very heart, which rejoiceth in God my portion more than the many do in the increase of their grain and wine. {Psa 4:7}
paragraphs.anchor: Said my soul.

paragraphs.text: Expectabo ut teneam per speciem, quem teneo per spem.
paragraphs.anchor: Therefore will I hope in him.

paragraphs.text: {a} Pet. a Figueir.
{b} Deicola Abbas.
{c} Emphatice loquitur.
Which few can skill of, and I have somewhat to do to hit on, but would not now have missed of for all the world. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: The Lord is good unto them that wait for him.

paragraphs.text: Not giving over till he findeth him.
paragraphs.anchor: To the soul that seeketh him.

paragraphs.text: {a} Et hoc apertam cruditionem continct. - Figu.

Heb., Be silent: not with a pythagoric or monastic silence, ut non liceat loqui locis et horis certis, but with a humble submission to God’s holy will, a patient and peaceable behaviour under his hand; waiting for a good use thereof, and a gracious issue in the best time - to frame the heart whereunto, Aurea his subnectitur sententia.
paragraphs.anchor: It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait.

paragraphs.text: The yoke of God’s law, and the discipline of afflictions: it is good to be betime in God’s nurturing house, and remain a good while there, that he be trained up in the school of afflictions, that he be a well-beaten soldier to the cross. {a} The description of such a one followeth.
paragraphs.anchor: It is good for a man that he bear the yoke from his youth.

paragraphs.text: {a} Quo semel iste imbuta reccus servabit odorem Testa diu. - Hor.
Sessio solitaria, as being much in meditation, according to that counsel of the preacher, "in the day of adversity consider."
paragraphs.anchor: He sitteth alone.

paragraphs.text: When God’s hand is upon his back, his hand is upon his mouth. See on Lam 3:26.
paragraphs.anchor: And keepeth silence.

paragraphs.text: Or, When he hath taken it upon him; taken up his cross, as being active in suffering.
paragraphs.anchor: Because he hath borne it upon him.

paragraphs.text: He lieth low at God’s feet: putting himself into the hands of justice, yet in hope of mercy. See 1Co 14:25.
paragraphs.anchor: He putteth his mouth in the dust.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Peradventure there is hope - q.d., doubtless there is; however, I will try, since I have lost many a worse labour.
paragraphs.anchor: If so be there may be hope.

paragraphs.text: Humility, the product of affliction sanctified, is still at her lesson, or rather practising what she hath learned. David, having suffered by Absalom, can well enough bear with Shimei’s tongue smitings; and the apostles, after they had been in prison, departed from the council, rejoicing that they were so far graced as to be disgraced for the name of Jesus. {Act 5:41}
paragraphs.anchor: He giveth his cheek to him that smiteth him.

paragraphs.text: He can bravely bear all contumelies and contempts for his conscience, taking them as crowns and confirmations of his conformity to Christ.
paragraphs.anchor: He is filled full of reproach.

paragraphs.text: No, not at all, however he may seem to some so to do. Non deserit etiamsi deserat, saith a father: He doth not put his people far from him, as the word here signifieth.
paragraphs.anchor: For the Lord will not cast off for ever.

paragraphs.text: As sometimes he doth "in very faithfulness," and that he may be true to his people’s souls.
paragraphs.anchor: For though he cause grief.

paragraphs.text: He will repent and return, and leave a blessing behind him, that is certain. {Joe 2:14}
paragraphs.anchor: Yet he will have compassion.

paragraphs.text: Heb., From the heart. {a} Non nisi coactus, as that emperor said when he sealed a writ for execution of a condenmed person: I would not do it but upon necessity. It goeth as much against the heart with God as it can do against the hair with us:
paragraphs.anchor: For he doth not afflict willingly.

paragraphs.text: “ Ille dolet quoties cogitur esse ferox. ”
{a} Non est Deo volupe, proprium, aut per se intentum. Poenas dat dum poenas exigit. - Sen. de Augusto. Iustis etiam suppliciis illacrymavit et ingemuit. - De Vespasiano Suetonius.

i.e., All those that are in misery, to lay more load upon them, and so to crush them to pieces, yea, to grind them to powder. This he could as easily do as bid it be done: but he takes no such delight in severity and harshness.
paragraphs.anchor: To crush under his feet all the prisoners of the earth

paragraphs.text: To wrest his right by false witness and corrupt means, as wicked men use to do before the face of the Most High, or of a superior under colour of law. God liketh none of all this, though again for excellent ends he allows it so to be, and orders it when so it is.
paragraphs.anchor: To turn aside the right of a man.

paragraphs.text: By sleight of hand to tilt the balance of justice on one side.
paragraphs.anchor: To subvert a man in his cause.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Seeth not. Non videt - i.e., non ei visum est, it seemeth not good unto him; he liketh it not.
paragraphs.anchor: The Lord approveth not.

paragraphs.text: Tam imprudens et imperitus? Can any one be so simple as to think that the enemy could do aught against us but by the divine permission and appointment? God, as he made all by his power, so he manageth all by his providence. This the Egyptians hieroglyphically set forth by painting God, (1.) As blowing an egg out of his mouth - that is, as making the round world by his word; (2.) To compassing about that orb with a girdle - that is, keeping all together, and governing all by his providence.
paragraphs.anchor: Who is he?

paragraphs.text: i.e., Prosperity and adversity; q.d., Who doubteth of that? {Amo 3:5 Isa 45:7} Talk not then of fate and blind fortune.
paragraphs.anchor: Out of the mouth of the Most High proceedeth not evil and good?

paragraphs.text: Mourn immoderately, or murmur causelessly. 1. If he mourn, let him mourn for his sin as the cause of his suffering; let him revenge upon that. 2. If he be tempted to murmur, let him remember that he is yet alive, and that is more than his part cometh to, since it is the Lord’s mercy that he is not consumed, and sent packing hence to hell. Life in any sense is a sweet mercy, even that which to the afflicted may seem a lifeless life. {as Pro 15:15} Let this patient us, that we are yet alive.
paragraphs.anchor: Wherefore doth a living man complain?

paragraphs.text: Heb., Man for his sin. For sin doth as naturally draw and suck punishments to it as the loadstone doth iron or turpentine fire; wherefore also the same word in Hebrew signifieth both.
paragraphs.anchor: A man for the punishment of his sins.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Make accurate inquiry into them; so shall we soon find ourselves to be a whole newly found world of wickedness. Search we therefore, and do it thoroughly. Many either search not at all (they cannot endure these domestic audits: it is death to them to reflect and recognise what they have done), or as though they desired not to find. They search as men do for their bad money; they know they have it, but they would gladly have it to pass for current among the rest. Heathens will rise up in judgment against such, for they prescribed and practised self-examination: Pythagoras once a day;
paragraphs.anchor: Let us search and try our ways

paragraphs.text: “ Non prius in dulcem declines lumina somnum,
Quam prius exactae reputaveris acta diei, ”& c.
Phocylides thrice a day, if Stobaeus {a} may be believed.

Let self-examination end in reformation, else sin will be thereby but emboldened and strengthened, as idle vagrants and lawless subjects are, if questioned only, and not punished and restrained. Of turning again to the Lord; {See Trapp on "Zec 1:2"}
paragraphs.anchor: And turn again to the Lord.

paragraphs.text: {a} Serm.

Holy hearts, pure hands. Instead of wrangling with God, {as Lam 3:39} let us wrestle with him in prayer; this is the only way to get off with comfort. Nazianzen saith, that the best work we can put our hands unto is, in coelos eas extendere, ad precesque expandere, to lift them up to God in prayer. But then it must be with a true heart. {Heb 10:22} See Job 11:13. {See Trapp on "Job 11:13"}
paragraphs.anchor: Let us llft up our hearts with our hands.

paragraphs.text: We have committed evil and omitted good, and failed in the manner, and are therefore justly punished. Let God hear such words fall from our mouths, set to work by our hearts, and then we may have anything.
paragraphs.anchor: We have transgressed and have rebelled.

paragraphs.text: Overwhelmed us with thy judgments. None out of hell have ever suffered more than the saints: they have felt the sad effects of displeased love.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast covered with anger.

paragraphs.text: Hid thy face from us, and secreted thyself as a judge doth when he hath passed sentence upon a malefactor, that he may not be solicited to reverse it.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast covered thyself with a cloud.

paragraphs.text: The veil of the temple was of no debarring matter, but thin and pervious, that the incense might easily pass through it into the Holy of holies: but now it was otherwise; God had set a bar between him and his people.
paragraphs.anchor: That our prayers should not pass through.

paragraphs.text: Eradicationem, saith the Vulgate; rasuram potius, not the rooting out, but the scrapings off. As the Jews did rather extrinsecus radere peccata quam intrinsecus eradicare, {a} shave off their sins outwardly, than root them out from within: so God made them as despicable as the parings of a pavement, or of a leprous house.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast made us as the offscouring.

paragraphs.text: See 1Co 4:13. {See Trapp on "1Co 4:13"}
paragraphs.anchor: And refuse.

paragraphs.text: {a} Bern. - Exverras, scobes et ramenta. Excreamenta et excrements.
i.e., Reviled and derided us. See Lam 2:16.
paragraphs.anchor: All our enemies have opened their mouths against us

paragraphs.text: Heb., A pit; great terror, and no way to escape. See Isa 24:17-18.
paragraphs.anchor: Fear and a snare is come upon us.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Mine eye descendeth; i.e., falleth, as it were, wholly away. See Lam 1:16; Lam 2:18.
paragraphs.anchor: Mine eye runneth down.

paragraphs.text: Put fire under the still, and water droppeth from roses. Fiery afflictions cause drops of repentance; and repentance, like the philosopher’s stone, maketh golden afflictions. {1Pe 1:7}
paragraphs.anchor: Mine eye trickleth down, and ceaseth not.

paragraphs.text: Let God but see the rainbow of sound repentance in our hearts, and he will soon shine forth, and cause it to clear up.
paragraphs.anchor: Till the Lord look down.

paragraphs.text: Iisdem quibus videmus oculis flemus, We see and weep with the same eyes. But Pliny {a} wondereth where that humour is at other times that floweth out of the eyes so readily and plentifully in case of grief.
paragraphs.anchor: Mine eye affecteth my heart.

paragraphs.text: Or, Prae omnibus filiabus, ‘More than all the daughters,’ &c.; more than the most passionate women use to weep when they are most grieved.
paragraphs.anchor: Because of all the daughters of my city.

paragraphs.text: {a} Lib. ii. cap. 32.
In a most eager and extreme manner, with utmost cruelty and craft.
paragraphs.anchor: Mine enemies chased me sore.

paragraphs.text: Beaten from bush to bush.
paragraphs.anchor: As a bird.

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah and the godly party might say so; but not Zedekiah and other perfidious ones.
paragraphs.anchor: Without cause.

paragraphs.text: Where I led a lifeless life; such as did Roger, Bishop of Salisbury, in King Stephen’s time, who sustained such miseries in prison, ut vivere noluerit, mori nescierit, that live he would not, and yet die he could not.
paragraphs.anchor: They have cut off my life in the dungeon.

paragraphs.text: As they did upon the mouths of dens, dungeons, or sepulchres, to make sure work. The Chaldee hath it, They stoned me.
paragraphs.anchor: And cast a stone upon me.

paragraphs.text: Many and great miseries have overwhelmed and oppressed me, both in body and soul. These are frequently compared to waters.
paragraphs.anchor: Waters flowed over mine head.

paragraphs.text: sc., From the land of the living; but God was better to me than my hopes.
paragraphs.anchor: Then I said, I am cut off

paragraphs.text: See Psa 130:1 Jon 2:1. {See Trapp on "Psa 130:1"} {See Trapp "Jon 2:1"}
paragraphs.anchor: I called upon thy name, O Lord, out of the low dungeon.

paragraphs.text: Seem a man’s case never so desperate, if he can but find a praying heart, God will find a pitying heart. Prayer is the best lever at a dead lift.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast heard my voice.

paragraphs.text: As breathing is a proof of animal life, so is prayer, though never so weak, of spiritual. If therefore you cannot speak, weep - fietu saepe agitur non affatu, tears also have a voice; {Psa 39:12} if you cannot weep, sigh - a storm of sighs may do as much as a shower of tears; if you cannot sigh, yet breathe, as here. God feels breath; and happy is he that can say, In te spero et respiro, In thee I hope, Lord, and after thee I breathe or pant.
paragraphs.anchor: Hide not thine ear at my breathing.

paragraphs.text: This thou hast done, and this I hope thou yet wilt do. Experience breedeth confidence.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou drawest near.

paragraphs.text: Whereof those Babylonians were no just judges.
paragraphs.anchor: O Lord, thou hast pleaded the causes of my soul.

paragraphs.text: It is the life, nay, the soul of the saints, that the wicked hunt after, though they do not always profess so to do.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast redeemed my life.

paragraphs.text: Thou hast seen it and art sensible of it; that is my comfort; for
paragraphs.anchor: O Lord, thou hast seen my wrong.

paragraphs.text: εχει θεος εκδικον δμμα.
As Psa 43:1.
paragraphs.anchor: Judge thou my cause.

paragraphs.text: See on Lam 3:59. The saints fare the better for their enemies’ spite and cruelty; and they may very well plead and present it to God in prayer.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast seen all their vengeance.

paragraphs.text: Their spiteful speeches and taunting terms have come into thine ears.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast heard their reproach.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Their contrivements. As the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers, {Psa 34:15} so he both seeth the ill carriage and heareth the ill language of graceless persons against the godly.
paragraphs.anchor: And all their imaginations.

paragraphs.text: See on Lam 3:61.
paragraphs.anchor: The lips of those that rose up.

paragraphs.text: Or, At their both sitting down (to eat), and at their rising up (from eatting). I am their music master, their table talk, and the matter of their mirth; they make sport with us, as the Philistines did with Samson. David complaineth of the like evil dealing. {Psa 35:15-17}
paragraphs.anchor: Behold their sitting down, and their rising up.

paragraphs.text: Call them to an account, and requite them. Let their music be marred, and the meal once ended, send them in a reckoning.
paragraphs.anchor: Render unto them a recompense.

paragraphs.text: In place of their mad mirth and sinful music; turn their psalm - as the Vulgate rendereth the word music in the foregoing verse - into a black santis, as they call it, ferale carmen, a doleful ditty. Dabis eis scutum cordis, saith the Vulgate. And, indeed, the word rendered sorrow signifieth a shield or cover. It noteth, saith one, the cardiaca passio, {a} whereby the heart is so oppressed, and there is such a stopping, that it is as it were covered sicut scute, as with a shield; there is a lid, as it were, put over the heart to keep off the most refreshing cordials, and so the heart is suffocated with sorrow. {b} It is as if he should say, Put them into such a condition that no creature may yield them the least refreshment. Spira was in this condition.
paragraphs.anchor: Give them sorrow of heart.

paragraphs.text: All the curses written and unwritten in thy book. This is not more a prayer than a prophecy. How effectual Christ’s curse is, may be seen in the withered fig tree in the Gospel, presently dried up by the roots.
paragraphs.anchor: Thy curse upon them.

paragraphs.text: {a} A Lapide.
{b} Mr Burrough’s Hos. Operculum cordis, vel apostema cordis.

Since they are thine and our implacable and irreformable enemies, be thou, Lord, implacably bent against them, to their utter destruction; and since they think us not worthy to breathe in the common air - whom thou hast made heirs of the world together with faithful Abraham our progenitor - destroy them from under these heavens of thine, in the compass and cope whereof thou reignest and rulest all.
paragraphs.anchor: Persecute and destroy them in anger.

paragraphs.text: Do thou, O Christ - to whom the Father hath committed all judgment - root them out from under the heavens of thy heavenly Father. Thus some paraphrase the words, and observe therehence the mystery of the Trinity; like as they do from Gen 19:24.
paragraphs.anchor: From under the heavens of the Lord.
